content: 1. Antibody responses can be observed in certain children as young as 3 months of age. However, a response comparable to that seen in adults is not typically achieved until children reach 4 to 5 years of age. The serogroup C component of the vaccine is poorly immunogenic in recipients under 2 years of age. 2. Polysaccharide meningococcal vaccines are effective in controlling outbreaks, with efficacy rates exceeding 85% among school-aged children and adults. 3. Serogroups Y and W-135 polysaccharides are safe and immunogenic in adults and children older than 2 years. Although clinical protection has not been definitively documented, vaccination with these polysaccharides induces the production of bactericidal antibodies. 4. The antibody responses to each of the four polysaccharides in the tetravalent vaccine are specific to their respective serogroups and function independently. 5. Individuals who have undergone splenectomy due to trauma or non-lymphoid tumors, as well as those with inherited complement deficiencies, exhibit acceptable antibody responses to polysaccharide meningococcal vaccines. 6. A 2003 study demonstrated that the tetravalent polysaccharide vaccine significantly reduced the incidence of invasive meningococcal disease in patients with terminal complement deficiencies compared to unvaccinated individuals with similar conditions. 7. Reduced clinical efficacy has not been observed in individuals who have received multiple doses of the vaccine. 8. The clinical significance of this immunologic hyporesponsiveness remains unclear. 9. Among infants and children aged 3 years or younger, the efficacy of the group A vaccine declines rapidly after vaccination. For example, among children vaccinated at 3 months of age, efficacy drops to less than 10% within 4 years. 10. Meningococcal polysaccharide vaccines have been widely used in mass vaccination programs, military settings, and among international travelers. Adverse reactions are generally mild, with the most common being pain and redness at the injection site, lasting 1 to 2 days. 11. Local reactions to the vaccine occur in 4% to 56% of recipients, while transient fever is observed in less than 5% of vaccinated individuals, more commonly among infants. Severe reactions are rare, with systemic allergic reactions occurring in 0 to 0.1 per 100,000 vaccine doses. Anaphylaxis has been documented in fewer than 0.1 per 100,000 recipients. 12. Neurologic reactions, such as seizures, anesthesia, and paresthesias, have been infrequently reported. 13. Bacterial polysaccharides, including those in the capsule of Neisseria meningitidis, are T-cell-independent antigens. These antigens do not elicit a memory response, as they stimulate mature B-lymphocytes but not T-lymphocytes. 14. Meningococcal polysaccharide vaccines have inherent limitations. The serogroup C polysaccharide is poorly immunogenic in children under 2 years of age, and the A polysaccharide induces an antibody response in infants, but vaccine efficacy declines rapidly. 15. These vaccines do not confer long-lasting immunity or significantly reduce nasopharyngeal carriage of N. meningitidis, limiting their ability to interrupt transmission and elicit herd immunity. 16. Conjugation of polysaccharides to a protein carrier containing T-cell epitopes transforms the immune response from T-cell-independent to T-cell-dependent. 17. Conjugate vaccines, such as those for Haemophilus influenzae type b (Hib) and Streptococcus pneumoniae, have successfully reduced the incidence of disease caused by vaccine-preventable serotypes and decreased asymptomatic carriage of the respective bacteria, thereby protecting unvaccinated individuals through herd immunity. 18. In the United Kingdom, monovalent serogroup C conjugate vaccines were introduced in 1999. A national vaccination campaign included a routine 3-dose infant series and a mass catch-up campaign targeting individuals aged 12 months to 17 years. 19. By 2001-2002, vaccine coverage in the UK was estimated at 80% among infants, 84% among toddlers, 76% among preschoolers, and 86%-87% among school-aged children. Vaccine effectiveness within the first year of vaccination ranged from 88% to 98% across different age groups. 20. Long-term data on the duration of protection are not yet available, but among infants who received three doses at 2, 3, and 4 months of age, efficacy declined significantly within one year. 21. The introduction of the vaccine led to a 66% reduction in carriage rates of group C meningococci in the UK and a 67% decline in serogroup C disease incidence among unvaccinated individuals aged 1-17 years, indicating the additional benefit of herd immunity. 22. The tetravalent meningococcal conjugate vaccine (MCV4), licensed in the United States in 2005, contains capsular polysaccharides from serogroups A, C, Y, and W-135 conjugated to diphtheria toxoid. It is available only in single-dose vials. 23. Studies among U.S. SBA titers greater than 4 are considered the standard correlate of clinical protection against serogroup C meningococcal disease.
